values.description: Replicas synchronize reference updates through coordinator-directed prepare, commit, and rollback phases.

values.label: Transactional Git reference updates
values.description: Git reference mutations use atomic, validated transactions that produce deterministic results and roll back completely on failure.

values.label: Consensus-free write acceptance
values.description: Any repository instance may accept writes, using storage-level atomic updates instead of elected consensus primaries.

values.label: Replica-distance reference-update limit
values.description: Geographic replica latency bounds sustainable per-repository reference-update throughput.

values.label: Reference-update amplification
values.description: Pull-request bookkeeping can multiply one user push into many additional replicated reference updates.

values.label: Slowest-replica consensus latency
values.description: Coordinated replication latency is bounded by the slowest participating replica.

values.label: Replica-count push-throughput degradation
values.description: Adding replicas reduces push throughput because consensus waits on more participants and their tail latency.

values.label: Per-repository reference-update latency budget
values.description: Replicated repositories must sustain several reference updates per second within a few-hundred-millisecond latency budget.

values.label: Per-write voting without a primary
values.description: Each write directly determines its winning order and outcome rather than following a primary's global ordering.

values.label: Rollback of non-majority writes
values.description: Writes failing majority agreement are reverted where applied to preserve surviving replica agreement.

values.label: Coalesced bookkeeping-update transactions
values.description: Bookkeeping reference updates are combined into fewer transactions to reduce cascading transaction load.

values.label: Priority scheduling for user reference updates
values.description: User-initiated reference updates take precedence over noncritical bookkeeping updates.

values.label: Consistency-and-partition-tolerance priority
values.description: Replica write coordination prioritizes consistency and partition tolerance over write availability.

values.label: Replica-based distributed locking
values.description: Replicas provide distributed locks that order coordinated database updates.

values.label: Overlapped replica-coordination work
values.description: The coordinator performs database, checksum, and lock work concurrently while replica communication is in flight.

values.label: Replica round-trip coordination latency
values.description: Multiple distant-replica round trips consume the write-coordination latency budget.

values.label: Durability-gated write acceptance
values.description: Writes are accepted only after the required number of replicas have synchronously committed them.

values.label: Write unavailability during replication shortfall
values.description: Writes become temporarily unavailable when the required replica count cannot be synchronously achieved.

values.label: Orchestrated push fan-out
values.description: An orchestrator distributes pushed packfiles and reference transactions to repository instances.

values.label: Unsynchronized packfile distribution
values.description: Pushed packfiles fan out without consensus because they are unreachable until references commit.

values.label: Single-local-repository synchronization
values.description: Reference transactions synchronize with one local repository rather than a replica quorum.

clusters.name: Replica Topology and Reconstruction
clusters.description: How many replicas and what replication architecture maintain repository durability?

values.label: Single-extra-copy replication
values.description: Keeps only one additional copy, sufficient for a single-node failure but insufficient for majority-based coordination of concurrent writes.

values.label: Spokes repository replication
values.description: Repository replicas are coordinated through the Spokes architecture to support geographically separated copies.

values.label: Three-replica repository replication
values.description: Each repository maintains a fixed floor of three replicas for consistency, redundancy, and continued push acceptance after one failure.

values.label: DRBD block-level replication
values.description: Repository filesystems are replicated at the block level through DRBD, requiring latency-close replicas.

values.label: Idle-replica resource overhead
values.description: A fixed replica floor consumes substantial resources on numerous small or inactive repositories.

values.label: Git-and-rsync replication
values.description: Repository content is replicated using complementary Git and rsync mechanisms.

values.label: Repository repair and rebalancing
values.description: Replication includes explicit operations to repair and redistribute repositories across file servers.

values.label: Non-voting geographic replicas
values.description: Geographic replicas serve reads and durability without voting on main-host write acceptance.

values.label: Rack-separated replica placement
values.description: Replicas are distributed so no two copies share a rack failure domain.

values.label: N-to-N replica reconstruction
values.description: After failure, repositories are reconstructed across arbitrary surviving sources and replacement destinations.

values.label: Periodic replica-count reconciliation
values.description: The system periodically restores each repository to its desired replica count.

values.label: Retirement through active-replica exclusion
values.description: A retiring server is excluded from active replica counts while replacement replicas are created.

values.label: Packfile-level application replication
values.description: Git data is replicated at the packfile and reference-transaction layer without distributing the Git implementation itself.

values.label: Git-level distribution
values.description: The architecture distributes or modifies Git itself to provide repository replication.

values.label: Fully consistent replica synchronization
values.description: All repository replicas remain synchronized so newly pushed commits are immediately readable everywhere.

values.label: Eventual-consistency repository views
values.description: Replicas expose repository state asynchronously, allowing some views to miss newly pushed commits temporarily.

values.label: Replica-consistency complexity cost
values.description: Maintaining synchronized replicas creates substantial system complexity as the cost of avoiding eventual-consistency failures.

clusters.name: Replica Read Verification
clusters.description: How is replica freshness, equivalence, and read-preserving behavior verified?

values.label: Optimistic gossip replication
values.description: Disseminate replica catch-up metadata through lossy gossip while relying on authoritative storage and read verification for correctness.

values.label: ETag-conditional replica read verification
values.description: Verify replica freshness against an object-storage index before serving reads, triggering catch-up when the index changed.

values.label: Globally consistent replica reads
values.description: Replica reads remain consistent despite lost replication messages or changing network topology.

values.label: Read-preserving replicated-write optimization
values.description: Replication write acceleration is designed without degrading the much more frequent repository reads.

values.label: Checksum-based replica state comparison
values.description: A checksum summarizes logical replica state for equality checking after updates.

values.label: Incremental XOR checksum maintenance
values.description: Reference changes update the logical-state checksum incrementally by removing the old pair hash and adding the new one.

values.label: Full checksum recomputation
values.description: Replica consistency checks recompute the checksum from all references for every update.

values.label: Checksum equality as logical-content equivalence
values.description: Equal replica checksums indicate equivalent logical repository contents.

clusters.name: Compaction Execution Locus
clusters.description: Where does repository compaction execute relative to primary and replica servers?

relations.reading: Choices on Compaction Execution Locus affect the outcomes of Planned Maintenance Availability
relations.rationale: The sources avoid replica-side repacking because its CPU cost can affect availability and can trigger failover when maintenance is accidentally performed on multiple nodes.

values.label: Primary-coordinated compaction
values.description: Runs compaction on the primary, records it in the WAL, and distributes completed packs so replicas do not repack locally.

values.label: Replica-side repacking
values.description: Allows each replica to generate compacted packfiles independently.

values.label: Replication-compaction coupling
values.description: Replication load and compaction work interact, affecting push throughput and replica read performance.

values.label: Git compaction throughput bottleneck
values.description: Git's on-disk compaction capacity becomes the limiting factor after object-storage latency is reduced.

values.label: File-handle scalability pressure
values.description: Unbounded pack-file growth strains clients because Git cannot keep handles open for all pack-files simultaneously.

clusters.name: Compaction Maintenance Technique
clusters.description: Which repacking and object-cleanup techniques maintain compact repository storage?

values.label: Background incremental maintenance
values.description: Repository maintenance runs incrementally in the background rather than blocking interactive operations.

values.label: Pack-count and storage reduction
values.description: Incremental repacking reduces pack-file count, storage footprint, and pack-management pressure.

values.label: Multi-pack-index maintenance
values.description: Maintenance creates and updates a multi-pack index so smaller background steps preserve efficient lookup across accumulated packfiles.

values.label: Single-pack full repacking
values.description: Maintenance consolidates all accumulated packfiles into one packfile through a full rewrite.

values.label: Loose-object cleanup
values.description: Maintenance removes accumulated loose-object storage to reduce disk and lookup overhead.

values.label: Pack-index scan growth
values.description: Accumulating separate pack indexes makes object lookup progressively slower.

values.label: Loose-object storage overhead
values.description: Accumulated loose objects consume extra disk space and impose performance costs.

clusters.name: Planned Maintenance Availability
clusters.description: How hosting servers are removed for planned maintenance while balancing shutdown speed against continuity of long-running reads and writes.

values.label: Quiescing before reboot

values.label: Immediate server reboot
values.description: Reboots or unplugs the server immediately, interrupting active operations such as large repository clones.

values.label: Two-copy degraded repository state
values.description: Unexpected server loss leaves repositories readable and writable with only two of three copies, but without tolerance for another failure.

clusters.name: Large-Repository Object Acquisition
clusters.description: How clients obtain Git data for very large repositories, contrasting complete transfer with demand-driven, server-assisted acquisition.

values.label: Complete object transfer
values.description: Transfers and verifies the full repository object graph during a conventional clone, creating substantial network, server, client, and latency costs.

values.label: GVFS demand-driven transfer
values.description: Initially transfers commits and trees, retrieves missing objects on demand, and can use nearby cache servers to reduce central-server load.

values.label: GVFS-style object-download cache servers
values.description: Separate fetch-object endpoints deliver packfiles while branch-update authority remains on central repository services.

values.label: Packfile-based Git networking
values.description: Push and fetch operations transfer Git packfiles over the network.

values.label: Packfile transfer availability limitation
values.description: Packfile-based transfer and filesystem dependence reduce availability when large storage or servers fail.

values.label: Partial clone transfer
values.description: Clients use partial clone to reduce large-repository transfer time and local storage when the hosting service supports it.

values.label: Standard-Git GVFS protocol support
values.description: The GVFS protocol is not incorporated into the standard Git client.

values.label: GVFS without cache infrastructure
values.description: GVFS deployment proceeds without the cache-server infrastructure required for scalable large-repository access.

values.label: Repository-size threshold for GVFS deployment

clusters.name: Working-Directory Population Strategy

values.label: Sparse working-directory population

values.label: Full working-directory population
values.description: Clone materializes all tracked files locally for users who need a complete working directory.

values.label: Separate source and build-artifact directories
values.description: Keep source files in a nested working directory while placing build outputs in sibling directories outside Git's managed tree.

values.label: Reduced working-tree management load
values.description: Minimize the files and directory state Git must manage during ordinary client operations.

clusters.name: Repository Placement and Read Routing

values.description: Any healthy server can materialize repository state without authoritative per-repository placement records.

values.label: Per-server repository location tracking
values.description: The system tracks repository placement on every server as authoritative routing state.

values.label: Rendezvous-hashed repository routing

values.label: Stale-routing recovery

values.label: External routing-database placement
values.description: Depend on an external routing database to locate repositories across hosting servers.

values.label: Geographically distant replica placement
values.description: Replicas are placed farther apart geographically to improve resilience and repository-population scalability despite inter-replica latency.

values.label: Closest sufficiently fresh replica routing
values.description: Reads route to the geographically closest replica that meets freshness requirements.

values.label: Single-replica read routing
values.description: After synchronized publication, each fetch or clone is routed to one repository replica rather than coordinated reads across replicas.

clusters.name: Hosting Failure Detection and Failover
clusters.description: How are server failures detected, represented, and handled during repository operations?

values.description: Heartbeats poll system load and confirm recovery, without serving as authoritative failure detection.

values.label: Primary heartbeat failure detection
values.description: Heartbeats serve as the primary authoritative mechanism for detecting failed nodes.

values.label: Operation-level replica failover
values.description: Each operation tries another preferred replica after a refused connection, timeout, or clean failure.

values.label: Advisory offline routing state
values.description: Offline status temporarily changes routing preference rather than authoritatively removing a node from service.

values.label: Replica retention after repeated failures
values.description: Repeatedly failing replicas move to the end of preference order instead of being removed.

values.description: Redirected RPC patterns are graphed to discover misbehaving or unavailable servers.

values.label: Per-application-server failure views

values.label: Live-traffic failure detection
values.description: Server liveness is inferred from live application traffic rather than a separate probe.

values.label: Failure-aware request routing
values.description: Requests are routed around servers detected as offline.

values.label: Isolation of losing replicas
values.description: Replicas losing a write vote are removed from service until repaired.

values.label: Automatic permanent-failure repair
values.description: Permanent disk or server failures trigger automatic restoration of repository replication.

values.label: Short-lived non-unanimous voting impact
values.description: Temporary replica disagreement usually resolves within minutes without visible availability loss.

values.label: Three-consecutive-request failure threshold

clusters.name: Client Repository Performance Strategy
clusters.description: How client-side Git performance is improved, contrasting integrated configuration and tooling with native Git scalability changes.

values.label: Integrated client optimization configuration
values.description: A managed client setup combines configuration, metadata acceleration, filesystem monitoring, fetching, and background maintenance for large repositories.

values.description: Large-repository performance is improved in Git itself through features such as commit graphs and sparse-checkout enhancements.

values.description: Client and repository performance bottlenecks are identified through custom tracing and analysis of user feedback.

values.label: Custom Git client extensions
values.description: Require a specialized Git client version to deliver repository-scale client performance features.

values.label: Background client maintenance
values.description: Run repository maintenance asynchronously and incrementally so interactive Git commands avoid expensive foreground work.

values.label: Foreground maintenance command blocking
values.description: Synchronous garbage collection delays ordinary interactive Git commands.

values.label: System-wide rewrite resource exhaustion
values.description: Large synchronous repository rewrites can consume CPU and memory and stall the entire client system.

values.label: Performance decay from deferred cleanup
values.description: Disabling automatic cleanup without effective background maintenance causes object accumulation and gradual performance deterioration.

values.description: Git uses a watcher that understands repository semantics such as ignore rules to avoid unnecessary scans.

values.label: Parallel checkout processing
values.description: Checkout work is processed in parallel to address checkout becoming a bottleneck after virtualization removal.

values.label: Core Git capability consolidation
values.description: Capabilities formerly supplied by Scalar or management layers are incorporated into core Git, reducing specialized client-layer dependence.

values.label: Virtualized filesystem client
values.description: A virtualized filesystem defers populated-size costs to improve large-repository client performance.

values.label: Foreground garbage collection
values.description: The client periodically performs garbage collection in the foreground during ordinary user work.

values.label: Scalar interim performance layer
values.description: Scalar supplies needed client performance temporarily while equivalent capabilities move into core Git.

values.label: Persistent Scalar dependency
values.description: Scalar remains a required long-term layer above Git for repository-scale client performance.

values.label: Working-directory inspection by core commands

values.label: Complete tracked-path index
values.description: The client index records every tracked path to support core command state inspection.

values.label: Updated large-index file format
values.description: An updated index representation reduces I/O and storage for millions of tracked entries.

values.label: Untracked cache
values.description: Git caches untracked-directory information to reduce large-repository inspection work.

values.label: Single-file index stream I/O
values.description: Index data is streamed through one file with cost dominated by sequential file I/O.

values.label: Multi-million-entry index
values.description: The client supports an index containing more than three million tracked entries.

values.label: Index compression from 400 MB to 250 MB
values.description: The updated index format reduces the stored index size and corresponding command I/O.

values.label: Hourly background repository fetch
values.description: Background fetches keep local objects current without placing download work in foreground commands.

values.label: Hidden remote-reference namespace
values.description: Fetched remote refs are kept under a hidden namespace for maintenance without changing visible refs.

values.label: Background split commit-graph maintenance
values.description: Reachable commits are maintained asynchronously in incremental split commit-graph layers.

values.label: Foreground-fetch overhead
values.description: Generating commit-graph data during foreground fetch adds user-visible fetch work.

values.description: Background graph generation includes every commit reachable through visible and hidden references.

values.label: Low average index-entry processing time
values.description: Large-index commands retain low per-entry processing cost because streaming I/O dominates.

values.label: Consolidated client maintenance command

values.description: Newly cloned repositories are automatically registered for recommended configuration and ongoing maintenance.

values.label: Compatibility-driven default-off performance features

clusters.name: Repository Hosting Model
clusters.description: Which broad collaboration and service model structures repository use: decentralized peer repositories or centralized hosted repositories.

values.label: Distributed repository workflow
values.description: Repositories remain peer-equivalent and support decentralized development, offline work, and delayed pushes.

values.label: Offline repository work

clusters.description: How are failed, missing, or retired repository replicas repaired, rebalanced, and replaced?

values.label: Repository repair and rebalancing
values.description: Replication includes explicit operations to repair and redistribute repositories across file servers.

values.label: N-to-N replica reconstruction
values.description: After failure, repositories are reconstructed across arbitrary surviving sources and replacement destinations.

values.label: Periodic replica-count reconciliation
values.description: The system periodically restores each repository to its desired replica count.

values.label: Retirement through active-replica exclusion
values.description: A retiring server is excluded from active replica counts while replacement replicas are created.

clusters.name: Replica Freshness Verification
clusters.description: How is a replica verified as fresh and safe to serve reads?

values.label: Optimistic gossip replication
values.description: Disseminate replica catch-up metadata through lossy gossip while relying on authoritative storage and read verification for correctness.

values.label: ETag-conditional replica read verification
values.description: Verify replica freshness against an object-storage index before serving reads, triggering catch-up when the index changed.

values.label: Globally consistent replica reads
values.description: Replica reads remain consistent despite lost replication messages or changing network topology.

clusters.name: Replica State Comparison
clusters.description: Which checksum or state-comparison technique verifies equivalence between replica contents?

values.label: Checksum-based replica state comparison
values.description: A checksum summarizes logical replica state for equality checking after updates.

values.label: Incremental XOR checksum maintenance
values.description: Reference changes update the logical-state checksum incrementally by removing the old pair hash and adding the new one.

values.label: Full checksum recomputation
values.description: Replica consistency checks recompute the checksum from all references for every update.

values.label: Checksum equality as logical-content equivalence
values.description: Equal replica checksums indicate equivalent logical repository contents.

clusters.name: Compaction Execution Locus
clusters.description: Where does repository compaction execute relative to primary and replica servers?

relations.reading: Choices on Compaction Execution Locus affect the outcomes of Planned Maintenance Availability
relations.rationale: The sources avoid replica-side repacking because its CPU cost can affect availability and can trigger failover when maintenance is accidentally performed on multiple nodes.

values.label: Primary-coordinated compaction
values.description: Runs compaction on the primary, records it in the WAL, and distributes completed packs so replicas do not repack locally.

values.label: Replica-side repacking
values.description: Allows each replica to generate compacted packfiles independently.

values.label: Replication-compaction coupling
values.description: Replication load and compaction work interact, affecting push throughput and replica read performance.

values.label: Git compaction throughput bottleneck
values.description: Git's on-disk compaction capacity becomes the limiting factor after object-storage latency is reduced.

values.label: File-handle scalability pressure
values.description: Unbounded pack-file growth strains clients because Git cannot keep handles open for all pack-files simultaneously.

clusters.name: Compaction Maintenance Technique
clusters.description: Which repacking and object-cleanup techniques maintain compact repository storage?

values.label: Background incremental maintenance
values.description: Repository maintenance runs incrementally in the background rather than blocking interactive operations.

values.label: Pack-count and storage reduction
values.description: Incremental repacking reduces pack-file count, storage footprint, and pack-management pressure.

values.label: Single-pack full repacking
values.description: Maintenance consolidates all accumulated packfiles into one packfile through a full rewrite.

values.label: Loose-object cleanup
values.description: Maintenance removes accumulated loose-object storage to reduce disk and lookup overhead.

values.label: Pack-index scan growth
values.description: Accumulating separate pack indexes makes object lookup progressively slower.

values.label: Loose-object storage overhead
values.description: Accumulated loose objects consume extra disk space and impose performance costs.

clusters.name: Planned Maintenance Availability
clusters.description: How hosting servers are removed for planned maintenance while balancing shutdown speed against continuity of long-running reads and writes.

values.label: Quiescing before reboot
values.description: Stops admission of new reads, completes existing reads, continues replication, and then reboots the server.

values.label: Immediate server reboot
values.description: Reboots or unplugs the server immediately, interrupting active operations such as large repository clones.

values.label: Two-copy degraded repository state
values.description: Unexpected server loss leaves repositories readable and writable with only two of three copies, but without tolerance for another failure.

clusters.name: Large-Repository Object Acquisition
clusters.description: How clients obtain Git data for very large repositories, contrasting complete transfer with demand-driven, server-assisted acquisition.

relations.reading: Choices on Large-Repository Object Acquisition affect the outcomes of Git Object Storage Backend
relations.rationale: The DHT design was undermined by Git’s packfile-based clone protocol, while GVFS changes which objects are transferred and when rather than merely changing server storage.

values.label: Complete object transfer
values.description: Transfers and verifies the full repository object graph during a conventional clone, creating substantial network, server, client, and latency costs.

values.label: GVFS demand-driven transfer
values.description: Initially transfers commits and trees, retrieves missing objects on demand, and can use nearby cache servers to reduce central-server load.

values.label: GVFS-style object-download cache servers
values.description: Separate fetch-object endpoints deliver packfiles while branch-update authority remains on central repository services.

values.label: Packfile-based Git networking
values.description: Push and fetch operations transfer Git packfiles over the network.

values.label: Packfile transfer availability limitation
values.description: Packfile-based transfer and filesystem dependence reduce availability when large storage or servers fail.

values.label: Partial clone transfer
values.description: Clients use partial clone to reduce large-repository transfer time and local storage when the hosting service supports it.

values.label: Standard-Git GVFS protocol support
values.description: The GVFS protocol is not incorporated into the standard Git client.

values.label: GVFS without cache infrastructure
values.description: GVFS deployment proceeds without the cache-server infrastructure required for scalable large-repository access.

values.label: Repository-size threshold for GVFS deployment
values.description: Repository size and user population determine whether GVFS and cache-server infrastructure are warranted.

clusters.name: Working-Directory Population Strategy
clusters.description: How clients populate tracked files locally, contrasting sparse default materialization with full working-directory clones.

relations.reading: Choices on Working-Directory Population Strategy affect the outcomes of Large-Repository Object Acquisition
relations.rationale: Sparse versus full population changes how much repository data clients initially download and retain, as documented by s05_p06 and s04_p02.

values.label: Sparse working-directory population
values.description: Clone initially materializes only a limited set of tracked files, commonly the repository root, while retaining on-demand access to other paths.

values.label: Full working-directory population
values.description: Clone materializes all tracked files locally for users who need a complete working directory.

values.label: Separate source and build-artifact directories
values.description: Keep source files in a nested working directory while placing build outputs in sibling directories outside Git's managed tree.

values.label: Reduced working-tree management load
values.description: Minimize the files and directory state Git must manage during ordinary client operations.

clusters.name: Repository Placement and Read Routing
clusters.description: How are repositories placed and requests routed to suitable hosting replicas?

values.label: Stateless repository placement
values.description: Any healthy server can materialize repository state without authoritative per-repository placement records.

values.label: Explicit repository-location tracking
values.description: An external routing table records the machines holding each repository copy and supports locating and validating those copies.

values.label: Per-server repository location tracking
values.description: The system tracks repository placement on every server as authoritative routing state.

values.label: Rendezvous-hashed repository routing
values.description: Repository IDs are mapped to expected healthy servers using rendezvous hashing, with placement adjusted as membership changes.

values.label: Stale-routing recovery
values.description: Routing may be stale after failures, and the system restores service by materializing repository state on a newly selected server.

values.label: External routing-database placement
values.description: Depend on an external routing database to locate repositories across hosting servers.

values.label: Closest sufficiently fresh replica routing
values.description: Reads route to the geographically closest replica that meets freshness requirements.

values.label: Single-replica read routing
values.description: After synchronized publication, each fetch or clone is routed to one repository replica rather than coordinated reads across replicas.

values.label: Single on-disk repository behind HTTP
values.description: An HTTP frontend serves one conventional on-disk repository from a single host.

clusters.name: Hosting Failure Detection and Failover
clusters.description: How are server failures detected, represented, and handled during repository operations?

values.label: Heartbeat-based routing load polling
values.description: Heartbeats poll system load and confirm recovery, without serving as authoritative failure detection.

values.label: Primary heartbeat failure detection
values.description: Heartbeats serve as the primary authoritative mechanism for detecting failed nodes.

values.label: Operation-level replica failover
values.description: Each operation tries another preferred replica after a refused connection, timeout, or clean failure.

values.label: Advisory offline routing state
values.description: Offline status temporarily changes routing preference rather than authoritatively removing a node from service.

values.label: Replica retention after repeated failures
values.description: Repeatedly failing replicas move to the end of preference order instead of being removed.

values.label: RPC failover pattern monitoring
values.description: Redirected RPC patterns are graphed to discover misbehaving or unavailable servers.

values.label: Per-application-server failure views
values.description: Each application server maintains its own offline list, containing network-local and application-local faults.

values.label: Live-traffic failure detection
values.description: Server liveness is inferred from live application traffic rather than a separate probe.

values.label: Failure-aware request routing
values.description: Requests are routed around servers detected as offline.

values.label: Isolation of losing replicas
values.description: Replicas losing a write vote are removed from service until repaired.

values.label: Automatic permanent-failure repair
values.description: Permanent disk or server failures trigger automatic restoration of repository replication.

values.label: Short-lived non-unanimous voting impact
values.description: Temporary replica disagreement usually resolves within minutes without visible availability loss.

values.label: Three-consecutive-request failure threshold
values.description: A server is marked offline only after three consecutive application requests fail.

values.label: False-positive node eviction
values.description: A healthy node can be temporarily marked offline after a coincidental run of failed requests.

clusters.name: Client Repository Performance Strategy
clusters.description: How client-side Git performance is improved, contrasting integrated configuration and tooling with native Git scalability changes.

values.label: Integrated client optimization configuration
values.description: A managed client setup combines configuration, metadata acceleration, filesystem monitoring, fetching, and background maintenance for large repositories.

values.label: Native Git scalability improvements
values.description: Large-repository performance is improved in Git itself through features such as commit graphs and sparse-checkout enhancements.

values.label: Repository performance tracing
values.description: Client and repository performance bottlenecks are identified through custom tracing and analysis of user feedback.

values.label: Custom Git client extensions
values.description: Require a specialized Git client version to deliver repository-scale client performance features.

values.label: Background client maintenance
values.description: Run repository maintenance asynchronously and incrementally so interactive Git commands avoid expensive foreground work.

values.label: Foreground maintenance command blocking
values.description: Synchronous garbage collection delays ordinary interactive Git commands.

values.label: System-wide rewrite resource exhaustion
values.description: Large synchronous repository rewrites can consume CPU and memory and stall the entire client system.

values.label: Performance decay from deferred cleanup
values.description: Disabling automatic cleanup without effective background maintenance causes object accumulation and gradual performance deterioration.

values.label: Git-integrated filesystem watching
values.description: Git uses a watcher that understands repository semantics such as ignore rules to avoid unnecessary scans.

values.label: Parallel checkout processing
values.description: Checkout work is processed in parallel to address checkout becoming a bottleneck after virtualization removal.

values.label: Core Git capability consolidation
values.description: Capabilities formerly supplied by Scalar or management layers are incorporated into core Git, reducing specialized client-layer dependence.

values.label: Virtualized filesystem client
values.description: A virtualized filesystem defers populated-size costs to improve large-repository client performance.

values.label: Foreground garbage collection
values.description: The client periodically performs garbage collection in the foreground during ordinary user work.

values.label: Scalar interim performance layer
values.description: Scalar supplies needed client performance temporarily while equivalent capabilities move into core Git.

values.label: Persistent Scalar dependency
values.description: Scalar remains a required long-term layer above Git for repository-scale client performance.

values.label: Checkout slowdown after virtualization removal
values.description: Sparse-checkout introduces slower checkout than virtualization because populated-size costs are no longer deferred.

values.label: Working-directory inspection by core commands
values.description: Core Git commands inspect on-disk working-directory state as part of repository operations.

values.label: Complete tracked-path index
values.description: The client index records every tracked path to support core command state inspection.

values.label: Updated large-index file format
values.description: An updated index representation reduces I/O and storage for millions of tracked entries.

values.label: Untracked cache
values.description: Git caches untracked-directory information to reduce large-repository inspection work.

values.label: Single-file index stream I/O
values.description: Index data is streamed through one file with cost dominated by sequential file I/O.

values.label: Multi-million-entry index
values.description: The client supports an index containing more than three million tracked entries.

values.label: Index compression from 400 MB to 250 MB
values.description: The updated index format reduces the stored index size and corresponding command I/O.

values.label: Hourly background repository fetch
values.description: Background fetches keep local objects current without placing download work in foreground commands.

values.label: Hidden remote-reference namespace
values.description: Fetched remote refs are kept under a hidden namespace for maintenance without changing visible refs.

values.label: Background split commit-graph maintenance
values.description: Reachable commits are maintained asynchronously in incremental split commit-graph layers.

values.label: Foreground-fetch overhead
values.description: Generating commit-graph data during foreground fetch adds user-visible fetch work.

values.label: Preserved visible branch references during background fetch
values.description: Background fetching updates objects while leaving local and visible remote-tracking branches unchanged.

values.label: Reachability-based commit-graph coverage
values.description: Background graph generation includes every commit reachable through visible and hidden references.

values.label: Low average index-entry processing time
values.description: Large-index commands retain low per-entry processing cost because streaming I/O dominates.

values.label: Consolidated client maintenance command
values.description: A single foreground command runs the repository maintenance steps together.

values.label: Automatic repository registration
values.description: Newly cloned repositories are automatically registered for recommended configuration and ongoing maintenance.

values.label: Compatibility-driven default-off performance features
values.description: Advanced performance features remain disabled by default to preserve broad compatibility.

clusters.name: Repository Hosting Model
clusters.description: Which broad collaboration and service model structures repository use: decentralized peer repositories or centralized hosted repositories.

values.label: Distributed repository workflow
values.description: Repositories remain peer-equivalent and support decentralized development, offline work, and delayed pushes.

values.label: Centralized hosted workflow
values.description: Organizations rely primarily on a central hosting service while retaining selected distributed-client capabilities.

values.label: Offline repository work
values.description: Clients retain the ability to work without contacting a central host.

values.label: Delayed repository pushes
values.description: Clients can accumulate work locally and defer pushing it to hosted infrastructure.

values.label: Hosting scalability difficulty
values.description: Large-scale Git hosting creates exceptional operational and architectural scaling difficulty.

values.label: Distributed-model and centralized-workflow mismatch
values.description: Distributed repository semantics can hinder organizations whose normal workflows depend on centralized hosting.

clusters.name: Git Object Storage Backend
clusters.description: Which backend stores and serves Git objects on hosting servers?

values.label: DHT-backed object storage
values.description: Stores content-addressed Git objects in a distributed hash table.

values.label: On-disk Git repository
values.description: Retains a conventional on-disk repository and standard Git tooling for object access.

values.label: Distributed-filesystem repository storage
values.description: Repository data stored through replicated or networked filesystem mechanisms rather than a conventional local repository.

values.label: Dedicated-fileserver RPC storage
values.description: Repositories remain on dedicated fileservers and applications access repository operations through remote procedure calls.

values.label: Filesystem-level distributed storage
values.description: Distribute Git data through a filesystem layer while retaining conventional Git repository access semantics.

values.label: Specialized Git implementation for unusual repositories
values.description: A custom Git fork operates on repository formats unlike standard on-disk Git repositories.

values.label: Network-filesystem performance and correctness degradation
values.description: Performance and correctness deteriorate when Git repositories rely on network-filesystem semantics.

clusters.name: Packfile Organization Strategy
clusters.description: How are stored Git objects organized and compressed in packfiles?

values.label: Size-minimizing packfile layout
values.description: Packfiles arrange objects primarily to minimize storage size rather than to follow object-graph locality.

values.label: Delta-compressed packfile objects
values.description: Most objects are stored as deltas within packfiles to reduce repository storage size.

values.label: Multi-pack indexed repository storage
values.description: Repository objects remain across multiple packfiles coordinated by a multi-pack index instead of being rewritten into one pack.

values.label: Multi-pack-index maintenance
values.description: Maintenance creates and updates a multi-pack index so smaller background steps preserve efficient lookup across accumulated packfiles.

clusters.name: Physical Repository Storage Distribution
clusters.description: How are repository data and packfiles distributed across disks and machines for capacity, parallelism, and availability?

values.label: Horizontal scalability without repository redundancy
values.description: Dedicated fileservers scale repository operations across machines while leaving each repository on a single machine.

values.label: Packfile availability limitation
values.description: Filesystem-resident large packfiles make repository access vulnerable to server or storage failures.

values.label: Packfile scalability limitation
values.description: Large packfiles and single-machine storage limit parallel operations and multi-server scaling.

values.label: Multi-disk and multi-machine repository placement
values.description: Repository storage is distributed across disks and machines to increase parallelism and survive server crashes.

clusters.name: Repository Persistence Architecture
clusters.description: How do repository mutations become durable and recoverable: through an integrated write-ahead log or an external transactional database?

relations.reading: Choices on Repository Persistence Architecture affect the outcomes of Replica Write Coordination
relations.rationale: The batch shows S3 WAL authority and ETag verification shaping how replicas catch up and serve consistent reads.

values.label: Write-ahead-log persistence
values.description: Persists repository operations in a WAL before acknowledging pushes and uses the log for recovery and replication.

values.label: External relational-database persistence
values.description: Uses blob storage for packfiles and a relational database for references and repository state.

values.label: S3-backed write-ahead log
values.description: Use object storage as the durable write-ahead-log source of truth for repository recovery and replica catch-up.

values.label: Simple storage-system architecture
values.description: Repository persistence uses a deliberately simple set of storage components for operational scalability.

clusters.name: Durable Write Acknowledgment and Publication
clusters.description: How are durable push acknowledgments and reference publication coordinated with persistence?

values.label: Durable push acknowledgement
values.description: A push is acknowledged only after its write-ahead-log entry is fully persisted.

values.label: WAL-indexed reference publication
values.description: References become visible only after their prepared transaction points to a persisted WAL entry in the WAL index.

clusters.name: Object-Storage Write Batching
clusters.description: How are repository object writes grouped and persisted in object storage?

values.label: Per-push object-storage persistence
values.description: Each pushed packfile and associated update is persisted as a separate object in object storage.

values.label: Batched object-storage writes
values.description: Object-storage writes are batched to avoid per-push PUT latency limiting throughput.

clusters.name: Replica Write Coordination
clusters.description: How are replicated repository writes ordered, committed, and accepted?

relations.reading: Choices on Replica Write Coordination limit the options available on Planned Maintenance Availability
relations.rationale: The system can reboot one server while writes continue because the remaining replicas can form the required majority; a weaker replication design would provide different maintenance guarantees.

values.label: Strict-majority coordinated writes
values.description: Uses three replicas, majority-held exclusive locks, strict-majority acceptance, and replica-wide serialization to prevent conflicting divergent writes.

values.label: Three-phase commit coordination
values.description: Replicas synchronize reference updates through coordinator-directed prepare, commit, and rollback phases.

values.label: Transactional Git reference updates
values.description: Git reference mutations use atomic, validated transactions that produce deterministic results and roll back completely on failure.

values.label: Consensus-free write acceptance
values.description: Any repository instance may accept writes, using storage-level atomic updates instead of elected consensus primaries.

values.label: Per-write voting without a primary
values.description: Each write directly determines its winning order and outcome rather than following a primary's global ordering.

values.label: Rollback of non-majority writes
values.description: Writes failing majority agreement are reverted where applied to preserve surviving replica agreement.

values.label: Consistency-and-partition-tolerance priority
values.description: Replica write coordination prioritizes consistency and partition tolerance over write availability.

values.label: Replica-based distributed locking
values.description: Replicas provide distributed locks that order coordinated database updates.

values.label: Overlapped replica-coordination work
values.description: The coordinator performs database, checksum, and lock work concurrently while replica communication is in flight.

values.label: Durability-gated write acceptance
values.description: Writes are accepted only after the required number of replicas have synchronously committed them.

values.label: Orchestrated push fan-out
values.description: An orchestrator distributes pushed packfiles and reference transactions to repository instances.

values.label: Unsynchronized packfile distribution
values.description: Pushed packfiles fan out without consensus because they are unreachable until references commit.

values.label: Single-local-repository synchronization
values.description: Reference transactions synchronize with one local repository rather than a replica quorum.

values.label: Read-preserving replicated-write optimization
values.description: Replication write acceleration is designed without degrading the much more frequent repository reads.

values.label: Replica-distance reference-update limit
values.description: Geographic replica latency bounds sustainable per-repository reference-update throughput.

values.label: Reference-update amplification
values.description: Pull-request bookkeeping can multiply one user push into many additional replicated reference updates.

values.label: Slowest-replica consensus latency
values.description: Coordinated replication latency is bounded by the slowest participating replica.

values.label: Replica-count push-throughput degradation
values.description: Adding replicas reduces push throughput because consensus waits on more participants and their tail latency.

values.label: Replica round-trip coordination latency
values.description: Multiple distant-replica round trips consume the write-coordination latency budget.

values.label: Write unavailability during replication shortfall
values.description: Writes become temporarily unavailable when the required replica count cannot be synchronously achieved.

values.label: Coalesced bookkeeping-update transactions
values.description: Bookkeeping reference updates are combined into fewer transactions to reduce cascading transaction load.

values.label: Priority scheduling for user reference updates
values.description: User-initiated reference updates take precedence over noncritical bookkeeping updates.

values.label: Three-replica repository replication
values.description: Each repository maintains a fixed floor of three replicas for consistency, redundancy, and continued push acceptance after one failure.

values.label: Idle-replica resource overhead

values.label: Git-and-rsync replication

values.description: Git data is replicated at the packfile and reference-transaction layer without distributing the Git implementation itself.

values.label: Replica-consistency complexity cost

clusters.name: Large-Repository Object Acquisition
clusters.description: How clients obtain Git data for very large repositories, contrasting complete transfer with demand-driven, server-assisted acquisition.

relations.reading: Choices on Large-Repository Object Acquisition affect the outcomes of Git Object Storage Backend
relations.rationale: The DHT design was undermined by Git’s packfile-based clone protocol, while GVFS changes which objects are transferred and when rather than merely changing server storage.

values.label: Complete object transfer
values.description: Transfers and verifies the full repository object graph during a conventional clone, creating substantial network, server, client, and latency costs.

values.label: Packfile transfer availability limitation
values.description: Packfile-based transfer and filesystem dependence reduce availability when large storage or servers fail.

values.label: Repository-size threshold for GVFS deployment
values.description: Repository size and user population determine whether GVFS and cache-server infrastructure are warranted.

values.label: GVFS demand-driven transfer
values.description: Initially transfers commits and trees, retrieves missing objects on demand, and can use nearby cache servers to reduce central-server load.

values.label: GVFS-style object-download cache servers
values.description: Separate fetch-object endpoints deliver packfiles while branch-update authority remains on central repository services.

values.label: Packfile-based Git networking
values.description: Push and fetch operations transfer Git packfiles over the network.

values.label: Partial clone transfer
values.description: Clients use partial clone to reduce large-repository transfer time and local storage when the hosting service supports it.

values.label: Standard-Git GVFS protocol support
values.description: The GVFS protocol is not incorporated into the standard Git client.

values.label: GVFS without cache infrastructure
values.description: GVFS deployment proceeds without the cache-server infrastructure required for scalable large-repository access.

clusters.name: Working-Directory Population Strategy
clusters.description: How clients populate tracked files locally, contrasting sparse default materialization with full working-directory clones.

relations.reading: Choices on Working-Directory Population Strategy affect the outcomes of Large-Repository Object Acquisition
relations.rationale: Sparse versus full population changes how much repository data clients initially download and retain, as documented by s05_p06 and s04_p02.

values.label: Sparse working-directory population
values.description: Clone initially materializes only a limited set of tracked files, commonly the repository root, while retaining on-demand access to other paths.

values.label: Full working-directory population
values.description: Clone materializes all tracked files locally for users who need a complete working directory.

values.label: Separate source and build-artifact directories
values.description: Keep source files in a nested working directory while placing build outputs in sibling directories outside Git's managed tree.

values.label: Reduced working-tree management load
values.description: Minimize the files and directory state Git must manage during ordinary client operations.

clusters.name: Repository Placement and Read Routing
clusters.description: How are repositories placed and requests routed to suitable hosting replicas?

values.label: Stateless repository placement
values.description: Any healthy server can materialize repository state without authoritative per-repository placement records.

values.label: Explicit repository-location tracking
values.description: An external routing table records the machines holding each repository copy and supports locating and validating those copies.

values.label: Per-server repository location tracking
values.description: The system tracks repository placement on every server as authoritative routing state.

values.label: Rendezvous-hashed repository routing
values.description: Repository IDs are mapped to expected healthy servers using rendezvous hashing, with placement adjusted as membership changes.

values.label: Stale-routing recovery
values.description: Routing may be stale after failures, and the system restores service by materializing repository state on a newly selected server.

values.label: External routing-database placement
values.description: Depend on an external routing database to locate repositories across hosting servers.

values.label: Closest sufficiently fresh replica routing
values.description: Reads route to the geographically closest replica that meets freshness requirements.

values.label: Single-replica read routing
values.description: After synchronized publication, each fetch or clone is routed to one repository replica rather than coordinated reads across replicas.

values.label: Single on-disk repository behind HTTP
values.description: An HTTP frontend serves one conventional on-disk repository from a single host.

clusters.name: Hosting Failure Detection and Failover
clusters.description: How are server failures detected, represented, and handled during repository operations?

values.label: Heartbeat-based routing load polling
values.description: Heartbeats poll system load and confirm recovery, without serving as authoritative failure detection.

values.label: Primary heartbeat failure detection
values.description: Heartbeats serve as the primary authoritative mechanism for detecting failed nodes.

values.label: Operation-level replica failover
values.description: Each operation tries another preferred replica after a refused connection, timeout, or clean failure.

values.label: Advisory offline routing state
values.description: Offline status temporarily changes routing preference rather than authoritatively removing a node from service.

values.label: Replica retention after repeated failures
values.description: Repeatedly failing replicas move to the end of preference order instead of being removed.

values.label: RPC failover pattern monitoring
values.description: Redirected RPC patterns are graphed to discover misbehaving or unavailable servers.

values.label: Per-application-server failure views
values.description: Each application server maintains its own offline list, containing network-local and application-local faults.

values.label: Live-traffic failure detection
values.description: Server liveness is inferred from live application traffic rather than a separate probe.

values.label: Failure-aware request routing
values.description: Requests are routed around servers detected as offline.

values.label: Isolation of losing replicas
values.description: Replicas losing a write vote are removed from service until repaired.

values.label: Automatic permanent-failure repair
values.description: Permanent disk or server failures trigger automatic restoration of repository replication.

values.label: Three-consecutive-request failure threshold
values.description: A server is marked offline only after three consecutive application requests fail.

values.label: Short-lived non-unanimous voting impact
values.description: Temporary replica disagreement usually resolves within minutes without visible availability loss.

values.label: False-positive node eviction
values.description: A healthy node can be temporarily marked offline after a coincidental run of failed requests.

clusters.name: Client Repository Performance Strategy
clusters.description: How client-side Git performance is improved, contrasting integrated configuration and tooling with native Git scalability changes.

values.label: Integrated client optimization configuration
values.description: A managed client setup combines configuration, metadata acceleration, filesystem monitoring, fetching, and background maintenance for large repositories.

values.label: Native Git scalability improvements
values.description: Large-repository performance is improved in Git itself through features such as commit graphs and sparse-checkout enhancements.

values.label: Repository performance tracing
values.description: Client and repository performance bottlenecks are identified through custom tracing and analysis of user feedback.

values.label: Custom Git client extensions
values.description: Require a specialized Git client version to deliver repository-scale client performance features.

values.label: Background client maintenance
values.description: Run repository maintenance asynchronously and incrementally so interactive Git commands avoid expensive foreground work.

values.label: Git-integrated filesystem watching
values.description: Git uses a watcher that understands repository semantics such as ignore rules to avoid unnecessary scans.

values.label: Parallel checkout processing
values.description: Checkout work is processed in parallel to address checkout becoming a bottleneck after virtualization removal.

values.label: Core Git capability consolidation
values.description: Capabilities formerly supplied by Scalar or management layers are incorporated into core Git, reducing specialized client-layer dependence.

values.label: Virtualized filesystem client
values.description: A virtualized filesystem defers populated-size costs to improve large-repository client performance.

values.label: Foreground garbage collection
values.description: The client periodically performs garbage collection in the foreground during ordinary user work.

values.label: Scalar interim performance layer
values.description: Scalar supplies needed client performance temporarily while equivalent capabilities move into core Git.

values.label: Persistent Scalar dependency
values.description: Scalar remains a required long-term layer above Git for repository-scale client performance.

values.label: Working-directory inspection by core commands
values.description: Core Git commands inspect on-disk working-directory state as part of repository operations.

values.label: Complete tracked-path index
values.description: The client index records every tracked path to support core command state inspection.

values.label: Updated large-index file format
values.description: An updated index representation reduces I/O and storage for millions of tracked entries.

values.label: Untracked cache
values.description: Git caches untracked-directory information to reduce large-repository inspection work.

values.label: Single-file index stream I/O
values.description: Index data is streamed through one file with cost dominated by sequential file I/O.

values.label: Hourly background repository fetch
values.description: Background fetches keep local objects current without placing download work in foreground commands.

values.label: Hidden remote-reference namespace
values.description: Fetched remote refs are kept under a hidden namespace for maintenance without changing visible refs.

values.label: Background split commit-graph maintenance
values.description: Reachable commits are maintained asynchronously in incremental split commit-graph layers.

values.label: Preserved visible branch references during background fetch
values.description: Background fetching updates objects while leaving local and visible remote-tracking branches unchanged.

values.label: Reachability-based commit-graph coverage
values.description: Background graph generation includes every commit reachable through visible and hidden references.

values.label: Consolidated client maintenance command
values.description: A single foreground command runs the repository maintenance steps together.

values.label: Automatic repository registration
values.description: Newly cloned repositories are automatically registered for recommended configuration and ongoing maintenance.

values.label: Foreground maintenance command blocking
values.description: Synchronous garbage collection delays ordinary interactive Git commands.

values.label: System-wide rewrite resource exhaustion
values.description: Large synchronous repository rewrites can consume CPU and memory and stall the entire client system.

values.label: Performance decay from deferred cleanup
values.description: Disabling automatic cleanup without effective background maintenance causes object accumulation and gradual performance deterioration.

values.label: Checkout slowdown after virtualization removal
values.description: Sparse-checkout introduces slower checkout than virtualization because populated-size costs are no longer deferred.

values.label: Multi-million-entry index
values.description: The client supports an index containing more than three million tracked entries.

values.label: Index compression from 400 MB to 250 MB
values.description: The updated index format reduces the stored index size and corresponding command I/O.

values.label: Foreground-fetch overhead
values.description: Generating commit-graph data during foreground fetch adds user-visible fetch work.

values.label: Low average index-entry processing time
values.description: Large-index commands retain low per-entry processing cost because streaming I/O dominates.

values.label: Compatibility-driven default-off performance features
values.description: Advanced performance features remain disabled by default to preserve broad compatibility.

clusters.name: Repository Hosting Model
clusters.description: Which broad collaboration and service model structures repository use: decentralized peer repositories or centralized hosted repositories.

values.label: Distributed repository workflow
values.description: Repositories remain peer-equivalent and support decentralized development, offline work, and delayed pushes.

values.label: Centralized hosted workflow
values.description: Organizations rely primarily on a central hosting service while retaining selected distributed-client capabilities.

values.label: Offline repository work
values.description: Clients retain the ability to work without contacting a central host.

values.label: Delayed repository pushes
values.description: Clients can accumulate work locally and defer pushing it to hosted infrastructure.

values.label: Hosting scalability difficulty
values.description: Large-scale Git hosting creates exceptional operational and architectural scaling difficulty.

values.label: Distributed-model and centralized-workflow mismatch
values.description: Distributed repository semantics can hinder organizations whose normal workflows depend on centralized hosting.

Fourth, the codes concerning repository checksums, repair scheduling, routing-table dependencies, and operational burden reveal a distinct large-scale repository health and repair-management decision. uncovered_concepts: Horizontal scaling through additional Rails instances
S3 Express One Zone storage tier
saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers the main repository-storage, WAL persistence, consistency, compaction, client-transfer, sparse-checkout, and client-maintenance choices. However, several relevant architectural axes remain uncovered. The application-tier architecture and scaling topology—retaining a Rails monolith while adding application instances—is distinct from repository placement and storage. The replica synchronization protocol is also more specific than the existing write-acceptance/consistency dimension: optimistic gossip dissemination, direct catch-up from an authoritative object store, and conditional freshness verification form a separate replication-recovery/read-validation choice. Elastic, per-repository replica sizing and eviction/materialization of idle replicas are distinct capacity and lifecycle decisions, not merely consistency choices. The choice among S3 storage tiers introduces a latency-throughput-cost axis absent from the generic persistence dimension. Finally, nested source directories with sibling build outputs represent a worktree/build-artifact layout decision not captured by sparse versus full working-directory population. The remaining codes are implementation details, forces, outcomes, or variants already subsumed by the existing dimensions, especially object storage, WAL persistence, compaction, sparse checkout, and client performance optimization.

uncovered_concepts: Heartbeat-based load polling and recovery confirmation
saturation_history.rationale: Most open codes are covered by existing dimensions: client watchers, sparse checkout, virtualization, parallel checkout, partial clone, cache servers, and Git maintenance fit Client Repository Performance Strategy, Working-Directory Population Strategy, Large-Repository Object Acquisition, or Repository Compaction Execution. Packfile constraints and placement alternatives fit Git Object Storage Strategy; Spokes' three-phase commit, replica count, latency effects, and write/read trade-offs fit Replica Consistency Coordination; and routing preferences and operation-level failover fit Repository Placement and Routing. However, the taxonomy lacks a distinct axis for the repository replication mechanism itself—block-level DRBD versus application-level Spokes replication—and lacks an axis for replica failure detection and membership-management policy. The heartbeat roles, advisory versus authoritative offline status, failure-based preference retention, RPC-pattern monitoring, and per-application-server failure views are not merely placement or write-consistency choices; they describe how failures are detected, represented, and acted upon.

The taxonomy covers the broader replication architecture, including application-level versus block-level replication, quorum durability, replica placement, routing, failure detection, repair, and consistency coordination. It also covers the client index, background maintenance, commit-graph updates, and fetch strategies under client performance and repository-population dimensions. However, it does not capture the distinct design decision of how replicas verify logical state equivalence after updates. The Spokes checksum mechanism introduces an uncovered axis: full recomputation versus incremental verification, including the checksum's reference-state composition, XOR aggregation, constant-time update formula, and the use of checksum equality as a logical-content consistency check. Existing ETag read verification is related but concerns freshness before serving reads, not per-update logical-state equivalence across replicas.

uncovered_concepts: Separate object storage for each pushed packfile
saturation_history.rationale: Most open codes are covered. Client-side configuration, core-Git consolidation, background maintenance, GVFS versus standard Git/partial-clone transfer, cache-server deployment, replica topology, consistency-versus-availability trade-offs, failure detection, 3PC, locking, local Git storage, WAL durability, and durable push acknowledgement are captured by existing dimensions. However, the taxonomy does not explicitly capture the WAL/object-storage write-path design axis: whether each pushed packfile is represented as a separate durable object and whether object-storage writes are individually issued or deliberately batched to remove PUT latency as a throughput limit. These are distinct from the choice of WAL versus database, the replica-coordination protocol, and Git packfile organization.
